opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there's something real there, but it's often overstated. The thing that seems true is that naive pretraining scale-ups have gotten somewhat less impressive per unit of compute than people might have extrapolated a couple of years ago. There were reports that some of the big training runs, the GPT-4.5-style runs, didn't deliver as much as people hoped relative to how much compute went into them. And there are real constraints: high-quality text data is getting harder to find, and building ever-bigger clusters takes time and a lot of capital.

But I'd push back on the framing of "a wall" for a few reasons.

First, the returns to pretraining were always roughly log-linear in compute. So you'd expect each increment to feel less dramatic in some qualitative sense even if the underlying trend is perfectly on track. People's vibes about "this model doesn't feel that much smarter" aren't a great measure of whether the scaling law broke.

Second, a lot of the action has just moved. Over the last couple of years, the biggest gains have come from RL on top of pretrained models: reasoning models, training on verifiable tasks like math and coding, agentic training. That doesn't mean pretraining stopped mattering. A stronger base model makes RL work better, and labs are still scaling both. It's more that the marginal dollar has shifted toward RL and inference-time compute because that's where returns have been highest lately.

Third, the measured progress on things I actually care about, like how long a task an AI agent can reliably do, has kept going at a pretty fast clip. If pretraining had truly hit a wall and nothing replaced it, you'd expect that to flatten, and it hasn't so far.

So my overall take is that pretraining scaling is somewhat slower and more expensive than the most bullish people expected, data is a real constraint, and compute buildout is going to be the binding factor over the next few years. But "AI progress has hit a wall" doesn't follow from that. I'd put a decent probability on progress slowing in the late 2020s as compute scaling becomes harder to sustain financially, but that's a different and more specific claim than "we've already hit a wall."

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the "wall" framing is kind of a mix of something true and something pretty misleading, and it's worth pulling those apart.

The true part is that the rate at which labs have been scaling up pretraining compute has slowed relative to what you'd have extrapolated from, say, 2020 to 2023. There's a bunch of reasons for that. One is just that the effective compute going into the biggest runs is getting constrained by things like building out the data centers, getting enough chips, power — the physical stuff. The other is that the returns from pure pretraining scaling, in terms of what you actually care about, looked a bit less dramatic than people hoped on some of the frontier runs in 2024. So there were reports that some of the big pretraining runs underperformed internal expectations. I think that's real, and I think there was a bit of a vibe shift at the labs where people went, "Okay, maybe we shouldn't just put all of our marginal compute into making the base model bigger."

But the misleading part is that people took that and concluded something like "AI progress is stalling," and that's just clearly wrong if you look at what actually happened. What happened is the labs shifted a lot of their effort into post-training, into reinforcement learning on tasks with verifiable rewards — math, coding, agentic stuff — and into inference-time compute. And the capabilities gains from that have been really large. If you look at the trend on things like the METR time-horizon benchmark, how long a task the models can autonomously complete, that's continued roughly on trend or arguably sped up. So the overall capability trend didn't hit a wall at all. It's more that the composition of where the compute goes changed.

And I'd add a few caveats on the pretraining side specifically. One is that I don't actually think pretraining scaling stopped working in the sense of the loss curves bending. The scaling laws still basically hold. The issue is more that going from, say, 10^25 to 10^26 FLOP gives you a predictable but modest improvement in loss, and it's unclear how much that cashes out in downstream capabilities relative to what you get from spending that same compute on RL. So it's a question of marginal returns, not of the approach being broken. The other caveat is that the biggest labs are still scaling pretraining — they're building the giant clusters, they're going to train bigger base models — it's just that the ratio of RL compute to pretraining compute is going up a lot.

Also, I think the data constraint thing is a bit overstated. People worry about running out of high-quality text, and that's a real consideration if you want to keep going up by orders of magnitude, but there are workarounds — synthetic data, multi-epoch training, and the fact that RL generates its own data in a sense. So it's a headwind rather than a hard stop.

So my overall take: pretraining scaling has slowed somewhat and the returns per dollar of just pretraining compute look lower than they used to, but it hasn't "hit a wall" in a way that matters for the question people actually care about, which is "is AI progress going to keep going fast?" And on that I think the answer is pretty clearly yes for at least the next couple of years, because there's a lot of room left in RL scaling, in algorithmic improvements, and in just the sheer amount of compute coming online. The thing I'd watch is whether the RL scaling also starts to show diminishing returns once labs have scaled it up by a few more orders of magnitude, because right now RL is at a much earlier stage on the curve than pretraining was, and that's a big part of why it's giving such fast gains.

astra-6.text:
I think “hit a wall” is a stronger claim than the evidence supports. It’s useful to distinguish between pretraining becoming less cost-effective and pretraining no longer producing meaningful improvements. You could have substantial diminishing returns and still get considerably more capable models by spending more.

There’s also a distinction between whether the pretraining loss keeps improving predictably and whether those improvements translate into capabilities people care about. Those aren’t exactly the same question. A model might improve on the training objective without becoming dramatically better at doing a long, complicated task reliably.

So I’d be uncertain about how much further pretraining alone takes us. But I’d be particularly skeptical of the inference that, if pretraining is slowing down, overall AI progress must be slowing down at the same rate. You can also improve post-training, spend more computation at inference time, and build better systems around the models. Those approaches have their own limitations, but pretraining isn’t the only thing that matters.

My bottom line would be: diminishing returns are plausible; a hard wall is a much stronger proposition. And neither, by itself, settles how quickly we should expect more capable AI systems to arrive.

sol-6.1.text:
I think “hit a wall” is a stronger claim than the evidence supports. There are several different claims that people run together here. One is that making the pretraining run bigger no longer improves the model’s prediction of text. Another is that those improvements aren’t translating into capabilities we care about. And a third is that the improvements aren’t worth the additional cost. Those are quite different possibilities.

You could have continued, fairly predictable improvements in the pretraining objective while getting less impressive gains on a particular benchmark. Conversely, a small improvement in that objective could make a model much more useful if it crosses some threshold for reliably doing a task. So I wouldn’t infer very much from a few benchmark results or from how impressive a particular release feels.

I’d also distinguish pretraining from the overall trajectory of AI capabilities. Even if pretraining started delivering substantially smaller returns, you could still get improvements from post-training, from having models spend more computation on a problem, and from building better systems around them. That wouldn’t establish that those approaches can compensate indefinitely, but it means a slowdown in one component isn’t necessarily a general slowdown.

So my view is uncertainty, rather than either “scaling is over” or “the previous trend must continue.” I’d want to see comparable runs at different scales, how their performance changes across a broad range of tasks, and what those gains cost. The claim that we’ve already established a wall seems premature.
